doc.title: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams Interview, 1967-05-13
doc.interviewee: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams

chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
title: Country suppers, quitting the blues, then prison, the dairy and release to Mr. Eastley
summary: In one long monologue Williams describes playing suppers and white parties, giving up the blues for church, prison captains who loved his playing, work at the dairy and with dogs, and being taken by Rudolph Eastley.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: That's the one you got now? No, that's not the one I got now. This was a assignment that I had. It sounded like an electric box. She sold it to me and she said, I paid, well, in that time, you could get a guitar, a cheap can, for about $50 or $60. She told me she'd pay $60 for that guitar. She said, that son of mine is not interested in you. She said, I said, for $4. She sold it to me. For $4? $4. So I'd taken that guitar and I went on, went on. I got more and more with it, you know? Which I used to then play the blues. I used to play, you know, what you call the white book music then. I was just about to forget it all. Then they'd tell me I'd run there. They'd come and get me to play for me. They'd bust their part and things like that, you know? And so from that on, I got on the blues and I was going to these country's suppers playing. Down half a night like that. And they got kind of interest in me. So I made pretty good living there. The thing was cheap then, you know? And at that time, you could take about $3 or $4 and go to the store. You couldn't pack your groceries back once you buy it in at the store. So I'd come and get plays then from Thursday to Friday, Saturday and Sunday, you know? Some of them would just, you know, just wouldn't put the price on what they got to pay me at the white folks' parties. They'd just pass their head around. Sometimes I'd get $7 or $8 out of the white folks just playing. Just passing their head around, you know? This country's suppers here, brother, kids, you know, well, they'd just set your price. Is that right? Right! Right! Right! And I'd pay you $2 or something like that. So after that night, I put my guitar aside and thought I was pre-Giant Church. I met a lot of church members who told me, say, quit playing the blues and you're Giant Church. Save your soul. When I did it, and maybe about a month, I could hear the sound of music coming to me. And then I'd go back and pick my guitar up and start back the plane. So, finally I just put it down, put it where I was for good one time, maybe about a year, and I didn't fool with it no more. But I couldn't leave it all the time. I just had to go back and get it again. Start the plane. So, when I had just let it fall, I guess you know what I'm talking about. One of those captains used to call me into the hallways. And they loved the blues, you know. And they'd play some more lonesome blues. Well, I'd go in and play them blues. And they would dial the telephone and let their family at the house listening to them. To make the blues. And they would say down there, what you having, a party or something? I'd hear them tell them on the phone, no, it's got Robert Pete Williams in there playing the blues. And they'd tell me, say, you know, good as you play a guitar. I said, you don't have no business here. He plays sad and he plays lonesome. He asked. They said, we're going to get you away from here, because you have no business here. But we can't get you away from here ourselves, like we used to could. But we'll have somebody to get you away from here. I told them I'd sure appreciate it. So, they kept me working in the field one week. And they took me out the field and they sent me to the milk dairy. And they told me, say, I'm going to send you down there. I said, but it's a mean man down there. He will hit you or he will kick you. But if you do that, say, just raise your hand and let the guards know you're coming in and come on back to the camp. I told them, yes, sir. He said, you think you can wait down there? I told them, yes, sir. I got down there to that dairy and they had cows you couldn't put the machine on. Well, I had to milk all of them by a hand. And that man be sitting in that chair. He was a mean looking man, Mr. Barney, though. How can I milk a machine? How can I milk a machine? That man sat there. He'd look at me. And when they would get up and come stand over me, I'd be wondering, what is I'm milking them right or something like that? When is he thinking hit me or kick me? So I'd get up and I'd go in to my milk, come back and get under one of the cows. I could find it when I come back in and strip them, see if I got milk dry, you know? He'd shake his head and then I got on the next cow. He said, I've seen a man milking, but I've never seen a man beat you milking a cow. He said, anytime a man can out a milking machine, I don't know what to say about it. He said, who lent you out a milking? I said, well, way back there in 29, I said, Mr. White, in a milk dairy, hired me to work for him. I said, I didn't know how to milk. I said, he lent me how to milk. Hired me to work for him for $3 a week, which is $12 a month. And I said, I've been working for him 15 years. I said, of course, he raised my wages from 12 to 20. I said, of course, you know the thing was cheap then. He said, well, you're really great. He said, I wish I had you on my phone out there. I said, you have the phone? He said, yeah. I said, what about it? He said, I went to Tash for Hope, Paris. Well, I told him, I said, I wish you could. Well, I passed on off and he had some dogs that he was raising up there on the phone, you know. And he told me, he said, Rob, you look like a good old donkey. I said, yes. He said, I want you to do something for me. I said, what's that? He said, I want you to train up my dogs. He said, well, let some of these other boys go ahead of you. And they're going to hide off and maybe get them a tree or something. Then you turn the dogs loose. Well, I do that. I run those dogs for that man. And they just, what if, you know. Leave off that. Those dogs hit that trail. They go get them a tree. Go right to that tree. Start up that tree and bark up there. So, Mr. Odom, he taken a liking to me, too. So, he told Mr. Barnard, though, that nothing happened to me down there. Because I was a quiet donkey. None of them fellas do me nothing. So, one day I run into the dogs. You know, you have to hold someone that had a belt on them, you know. Well, running through the bush, I got struck in the eye. And so, Mr. Odom come down there. He said, what's the matter with his eyes? So, Mr. Barnard told him. Well, he called me in the office. I had to be up there. He said, ain't nobody jumped on you. I told him, no, sir. He said, well, I'll tell you before, Mr. Barnard. I don't want nobody hitting on me. Nobody. He said, if they do, he said, you see me. He said, I got a brother up there in North, Louisiana. He said, I'm going to get you out of here and send you to my brother. I said, you got a good record. I killed a lot about you myself. But he didn't get a chance to get me. And man, over in Dunnip Springs, Mr. Eastley got me. Yes, sir. So, as you used to come up there, they had Mr. Austin come up there. He came up there and he actually called me, I make Family Blues. I made that Family Blues with 12th, Frank Getty. And then he actually called me to the governor of the church song. Well, I did that. When I had the church song, they carried that to the boat. And then carrying that church song to the boat, Mr. Rudolph Eastley came up there and got me. I used to tell those people all the time, I said, I won't be here long. They said, oh, man like you with a fresh life. They're talking about you ain't going to be here long, ain't been here no time. I said, just forget about that. I said, I got a man that's going to help me. Who is that man? I said, that man up there. That means Jesus Christ. Some of them had to know, they said, oh, we don't think about Jesus Christ, because it ain't no God. I've been here 20-something years and they ain't gone nowhere yet. I said, well, you all just sit here and kill one another and fight and go on. I said, I'm leaving here. Well, okay.
